title: SSH and secure remote access
description: Troubleshoot SSH connectivity, authentication, and secure access patterns.

data.text: SSH (Secure Shell) is the standard way to access Linux servers remotely. When you cannot connect to a server, the problem could be DNS, a firewall, SSH daemon configuration, or your local SSH client. Understanding the SSH workflow helps you isolate the issue quickly.

SSH uses encryption to protect the connection. The client and server negotiate a shared secret using public-key cryptography. Once the encrypted channel is established, your password or key is transmitted securely. This is why SSH is the default for production server access.

When you run ssh user@server, the client first resolves the server hostname to an IP address using DNS. It then establishes a TCP connection on port 22. The server presents its host key, the client verifies it, and then the client authenticates using a password or private key.

items: DNS resolution: the hostname must resolve to the correct IP
TCP handshake: port 22 must be reachable
SSH handshake: the server must be running sshd
Authentication: password, public key, or other method must succeed

data.text: SSH has a built-in verbose mode that shows exactly what is happening at each step. This is the first thing to run when a connection fails. It will tell you if DNS failed, if the TCP connection was refused, if the key exchange failed, or if authentication was rejected.

data.code:
ssh -vvv user@server
# Check if sshd is running on the server
systemctl status sshd
# Test connectivity
nc -zv server 22

data.text: Password authentication is simple but less secure and harder to automate. Key-based authentication uses a private key on your machine and a public key on the server. The private key never leaves your machine. You can protect the private key with a passphrase for extra security.

data.title: SSH configuration file
data.text: The ~/.ssh/config file lets you define shortcuts and options per host. You can set User, IdentityFile, Port, and ProxyJump in one place. This avoids typing long commands and reduces mistakes.

items: Connection refused: sshd is not running or a firewall is blocking port 22
Permission denied: wrong password, wrong key, or user is not in AllowUsers
Host key changed: the server was reinstalled or its key rotated; update known_hosts
Too many authentication failures: you offered too many keys; use IdentitiesOnly yes

data.title: Key Takeaways
items: SSH connects over TCP port 22 using encrypted handshakes
Use ssh -vvv to see exactly what is failing
Key-based authentication is more secure and automatable than passwords
Check sshd status, firewall rules, and DNS when connection fails
